description: We’re taking on the Dancing with the SARs challenge to combine electrical engineering, coding and AI into one project. Join us!
summary: SlopeWatch is a research prototype that asks whether satellite radar recorded unusual change on a mountain slope before it failed. Our case study is the rock-and-ice collapse on Langtang Lirung, Nepal, on 26 August 2026. Using public NASA-ISRO NISAR standard products, we found that a 0.056 km² patch on the slope shows a wrapped-phase step equivalent to 4.7–5.6 cm along the radar line of sight between 14 and 26 July, one month before the collapse. None of 361 comparable control slopes nearby showed a step that large in that pair. A simple "new movement" rule run over a year of passes flags the Langtang slope once, and raises 268 other flags that are still unverified. NISAR backscatter and Sentinel-1 brightness then show strong surface change across the collapse itself. We present this in an interactive story page and map explorer, with all code, numbers and negative results in an open repository. SlopeWatch is a retrospective analysis, not a warning service: we have not confirmed that the signal is ground movement, and the method was tuned on this one event. It shows how NISAR data could support a watch list for expert review of high-mountain hazards.
details:
What it does: SlopeWatch examines what NASA-ISRO NISAR radar recorded before and after the Langtang Lirung collapse in Nepal (26 August 2026) and tests whether the same simple rule could build a watch list of slopes for expert review. It has two parts: a reproducible Python analysis pipeline and a static website with a scroll-through story page and an interactive map explorer covering one year of radar passes.

How it works: We read the 20 m wrapped interferogram layer in NISAR GUNW standard products and measure the phase step on a fixed 0.056 km² patch against five reference areas and up to 361 comparable control slopes in a 30 km window. A "new movement" detector flags places that were quiet in earlier passes and then show a compact anomaly. NISAR GCOV backscatter, Sentinel-1 interferograms, OPERA RTC-S1 brightness and HLS optical scenes are used to check the result and to look at the collapse itself.

What we found: A phase step equivalent to 4.7–5.6 cm line of sight in 14–26 July, larger than every control slope in that pair. The 80 m unwrapped layer discards this patch, so processing choices decide whether the signal is visible. Backscatter change inside the UNOSAT-mapped footprint rises from 18.6% to 41.2% of pixels across the collapse, and Sentinel-1 brightness drops 12.0 dB and 10.6 dB on two tracks. The detector raised 270 flags over 22 pairs; 268 are unverified.

Benefits and intended impact: a transparent evidence package that helps specialists decide which high-mountain slopes deserve attention, and that makes gaps in satellite observation visible to people responsible for downstream communities, roads and hydropower.

What we considered: honesty about limits. The final 24 days before the collapse are unresolved, a plausible seasonal Sentinel-1 signal was tested and rejected, and the detector was tuned on Langtang, so this is a development case and not proof of prediction. Negative results are published with the positive ones.

Tools: Python (numpy, scipy, Pillow, h5py, fsspec, requests, pytest), NASA Earthdata, CMR and the Alaska Satellite Facility for data access, Leaflet with plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the website, GitHub and Vercel for hosting. AI assistants (Claude and Codex) were used for coding, analysis support and review; this is recorded in the repository.

Code, methods and every number: https://github.com/Hamza-Atiq/dancing-with-the-sars
dataRefs: NISAR GUNW, GCOV and GOFF products (NASA-ISRO, via Alaska Satellite Facility DAAC)
NASA Earthdata and Common Metadata Repository (CMR) search
OPERA RTC-S1 (radiometric terrain corrected Sentinel-1 backscatter)
